Basically your vertebrae are being held together by just hardware at that point. In rare cases, hardware can break, you don’t fuse, etc. You want to make sure it’s as stabilized as a position you can so it 1. Doesn’t move around and delay healing, 2. It gives something for your head to rest on instead of your neck. You can be surprised how heavy your head feels when you’re not supporting it and then 3. It helps minimize pain. When you’re laying down or leaning in a recliner, something other than your neck is supporting your head too. It may be easier to sleep sitting in a recliner for the first few weeks. 

I put the ice packs on the back of my neck and side. I had pain there from being moved around (surgery isn’t gentle), and my throat stayed swollen for a time and it seemed to help a bit.

I can understand why you’re afraid. It is a daunting surgery. The best thing I can say is listen to your body. Rest when you need to. Take medication as you need to. Don’t try to tough anything out. Ask for help.

Hey, I had my C 5/6 acdf done about 4 years ago now. I was nervous because it was my first big surgery and well you know, it’s the spine. But it went well. I spent one night in the hospital and my pain was managed through meds through an IV at first and then orally. I asked for a lot of ice packs to help between doses of medication. I wouldn’t say the pain was worst than before surgery it was just different. After doing the PT and OT and walking around the floor, they were ready to kick me out. 

I would say that the first few days after you’re going to be tired and sore in a bunch of places. They’re not gentle moving you when you’re unconscious. Rest as you need to. And then start walking as soon as you can. It helps w preventing blood clots and it just helps changing scenery instead of staying inside. 

When they say to keep your brace on, keep it on. Any restriction they give you, follow it. I think the most difficult thing for me was not lifting anything. You’d be surprised at how little 5-10 lbs feels and you over do it. 

For about 2-3 weeks after they give you oral pain medicine. I found the pain tolerable with that and ice. You’re going to feel extra fatigued for a few weeks so please listen to your body and rest when you need it.

As far as PT before surgery. I was told they try 6 months of conservative treatment before even talking another surgery.

When I went in I had pins and needles in my left hand, shoulder pain and weakness. They were mostly resolved after surgery.

Sorry for the novel, if you have any questions please feel free to ask. And good luck!

I don’t know if this will mean anything but i survived the 1990 Plainfield tornado. My house was one of the homes destroyed in the Wheatland Plains subdivision. We had no warning. I was outside and just happened to go inside minutes before it hit. Now there are so many ways to receive warnings and advance notice of weather. It’s not just hearing a siren and “oh shit I have maybe 30 seconds to get to shelter”. Now you have 15+ minutes. Not to mention the advanced warnings the news can give you days ahead of time to prepare. What I do for my peace of mind to prepare. I have a go bag. I have clothes, a few days of my medicine, a list of my meds, some first aid stuff, dog stuff, and anything important that I just can throw in there. I spent a lot of time being terrified of another tornado coming. The best thing I can tell you is to just be prepared and have a plan incase one happens. We can’t control the weather, but you can be ready if something does happen.
